Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: Northstar AI x Redwood — Dedicated PoC check-in (week 1)
Date: 2025-03-06 5:00 PM PT
Duration: 34 min
Attendees: Stephanie Nguyen (Redwood), Markus Klein (Redwood), Ethan Park (Redwood), Maya Patel (Northstar AI), Connor Lee (Northstar AI), Elena Ruiz (Northstar AI)

Summary:
- Reviewed week 1 PoC benchmark results on Dedicated pool. Throughput is trending in the right direction after enabling continuous batching, but p99 latency still spikes under bursty concurrency.
- Discussed tuning: max concurrent sequences, batch token caps, and queue delay target; also enabling prefix/prompt caching to reduce TTFT for repeated system prompts.
- Talked through commit sizing for production: use observed 7-day tokens plus expected Q2 event peak; consider headroom and multi-region needs.

Topics:
1) Benchmark results recap (before/after batching)
2) Latency and queueing behavior under burst load
3) Caching options (prefix cache / KV cache behavior)
4) Commit sizing + next-week success criteria

Action items:
- Redwood to send config recommendations and enable prefix caching on PoC route.
- Northstar to re-run load test with fixed prompt set and share raw output.
- Stephanie to send a commit sizing proposal with assumptions.

Questions:
- What p99 SLO matters more: end-user latency or internal queue time stability?
- Do you need VPC connectivity for production, or is IP allowlist sufficient for initial rollout?


Transcript:

[00:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Cool, alright, I think we’re all here. Maya, Connor, Elena — good to see you again. Markus and Ethan are on from our side.

[00:10] Maya Patel: Hey, yep. Thanks for making time.

[00:12] Markus Klein: Hey everyone.

[00:13] Ethan Park: Hi.

[00:15] Stephanie Nguyen: Goal today: week one check-in, review the benchmark numbers you sent, talk about tuning batching and caching, and then start to outline what commit sizing might look like if this goes to prod. Sound okay?

[00:28] Maya Patel: Yeah. We’re also trying to understand what knobs we can safely change without… like, surprising quality. But mostly it’s latency.

[00:36] Stephanie Nguyen: Perfect. Connor, do you want to start with what you saw?

[00:40] Connor Lee: Sure. So we ran the same harness as last week — 200 concurrent max, ramp up over like 3 minutes. Using the chat endpoint, streaming on. The good news is tokens per second went up when we applied your “continuous batching” settings.

[00:56] Connor Lee: But the p99 is still kind of nasty once we hit the ramp. We had p50 around 750 milliseconds to first token, p95 around 1.9 seconds, and p99 jumped to like 7-ish seconds. That’s too high for our UX.

[01:11] Markus Klein: Got it. And to be clear, those are TTFT numbers, not full completion time, right?

[01:16] Connor Lee: Yeah. Time to first token.

[01:18] Elena Ruiz: And during that p99 spike, we also saw a few timeouts on the client side. Not a ton, but enough to worry.

[01:26] Ethan Park: Do you recall your client timeout setting?

[01:29] Elena Ruiz: It’s 10 seconds on the gateway, 15 on the service.

[01:33] Markus Klein: Okay, thanks. On the throughput side, what did you see — like total output tok/sec?

[01:39] Connor Lee: In the run we shared, average was around 2.3k output tokens per second across the whole pool. It’s a little fuzzy because of streaming, but that’s the number.

[01:48] Markus Klein: That’s helpful.

[01:50] Stephanie Nguyen: And the baseline before the batching config, what was it?

[01:54] Connor Lee: Like 1.6k-ish. So the improvement is real.

[01:58] Maya Patel: The other thing is, our traffic isn’t a clean ramp. It’s spiky. We have an internal job that kicks off and then you get like 300 requests within 20 seconds.

[02:08] Markus Klein: Yeah, that’s the “burst concurrency” problem, and that’s usually where queueing and batch formation can make p99 look scary.

[02:16] Ethan Park: Also depends on max_num_seqs versus your average prompt length. If the prompts are longer than we assumed, the batcher can behave differently.

[02:24] Connor Lee: Our prompts are like… system prompt is pretty long. It’s about 900 tokens. Then user query is small, 50 to 100. And we have a few tool descriptions.

[02:35] Markus Klein: That’s actually a good candidate for prefix caching, because that 900 token system prompt repeats a lot, right?

[02:41] Maya Patel: Yes. It repeats across basically all requests. We have minor variations, but it’s mostly stable.

[02:47] Markus Klein: Great. So two buckets of improvements: batching knobs to handle the burst, and caching to reduce TTFT when prompt repeats.

[02:57] Stephanie Nguyen: Markus, can you walk them through what knobs we’d adjust next?

[03:01] Markus Klein: Yep. In plain terms, we control: (1) how long we’re willing to wait to form a batch, (2) how many sequences we’ll batch together, (3) how many tokens we allow in one batch, and then (4) concurrency caps.

[03:15] Markus Klein: For spiky bursts, you want a small queue delay target — like 5 to 15 milliseconds — so you’re not sitting around waiting to batch while p99 blows up. But you still want enough batch size to keep GPUs busy.

[03:28] Elena Ruiz: So if we lower the queue delay, do we lose throughput?

[03:31] Markus Klein: Usually a bit, yes, but it can be the right trade if you care about p99.

[03:36] Connor Lee: The config we used was max batch tokens 8192 and max num sequences 32. Is that right?

[03:43] Ethan Park: That’s what I see in the deployment config, yeah.

[03:46] Markus Klein: For 900-token prompts, 8192 might be forcing smaller effective batches than you think, because prompt + generation both count.

[03:54] Connor Lee: Oh. So it’s basically saturating on prompt tokens.

[03:58] Markus Klein: Exactly. So one path: increase max_batch_tokens. But then you have to watch memory and also the effect on tail latency.

[04:07] Maya Patel: We also saw memory pretty high on the nodes. Like 82%.

[04:11] Ethan Park: That lines up. You’re doing long prompts, plus KV cache grows with sequence length. So we can adjust for that too.

[04:20] Stephanie Nguyen: And caching might take pressure off, because if you can reuse that prefix you’re not re-processing those 900 tokens each time.

[04:27] Connor Lee: How does your prefix cache work? Is it like… literally caching the KV?

[04:32] Ethan Park: It’s effectively reusing computed prefix states, yes. It’s not “token cache” like HTTP caching. It’s model-specific and tied to the prompt prefix.

[04:42] Connor Lee: So would it break if we have tool definitions that change?

[04:45] Markus Klein: If the prefix changes, cache miss. If it’s stable, you’ll get hits.

[04:50] Maya Patel: Our tool schema changes like once a week, but not per request. So it should still help.

[04:57] Markus Klein: Great.

[05:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Ethan, can we enable prefix caching for the PoC route this week?

[05:05] Ethan Park: Yes. We can turn it on and then we’ll share how to read the cache hit rate metrics.

[05:11] Elena Ruiz: That’s a metric you expose?

[05:13] Ethan Park: In the console, yes — cache hit, miss, and estimated tokens saved. Sometimes it’s delayed by a few minutes.

[05:20] Elena Ruiz: That’s fine.

[05:22] Connor Lee: On the p99 spikes, can you help us interpret if it’s queue time or compute time?

[05:27] Markus Klein: Yep. The easiest is to look at server-side breakdown: queue delay, prefill time, decode time. If the p99 is mostly queue, we tune batching/concurrency. If it’s prefill, caching helps. If it’s decode, it might be generation length variability.

[05:43] Connor Lee: We do have variable generation. Max tokens 512, but sometimes it goes to like 400.

[05:49] Markus Klein: That’ll contribute to decode tail. One trick is to separate routes: interactive route with lower max tokens, and a background route for long generations.

[05:59] Maya Patel: That’s interesting. We haven’t split it. We could.

[06:03] Stephanie Nguyen: If that’s in scope for your product, it’s often the easiest win.

[06:09] Maya Patel: Yeah, we can.

[06:11] Markus Klein: Also, when you have spiky bursts, you can cap concurrency to keep the system stable, and let the client backoff. But that’s a product decision.

[06:22] Elena Ruiz: We’d rather not 429 customers.

[06:25] Markus Klein: Totally. That’s why Dedicated helps versus shared. But even on Dedicated you can overload it.

[06:33] Stephanie Nguyen: Which gets us to commit sizing. If the peak is 300 requests in 20 seconds, we need to decide: do you want to provision for that peak, or allow some queueing.

[06:44] Maya Patel: For the end-user path we want it to feel snappy. For internal jobs, it can queue.

[06:49] Stephanie Nguyen: Great, so we can define two SLOs.

[06:52] Connor Lee: For snappy, we want p95 under 2 seconds TTFT, p99 under 4 seconds.

[06:59] Markus Klein: Okay. That’s doable.

[07:01] Ethan Park: With caching on, you might see TTFT drop quite a bit because prefill becomes smaller.

[07:07] Connor Lee: That would be huge.

[07:10] Stephanie Nguyen: Let’s talk numbers. You shared last week you’re around… what, 45 million tokens a day?

[07:17] Maya Patel: Roughly. It’s growing.

[07:19] Stephanie Nguyen: And that’s total input+output?

[07:21] Maya Patel: Total.

[07:23] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay. So for a commit we usually frame it in capacity units that translate to tokens/sec at your prompt distribution. The reason is: tokens/day doesn’t capture burst.

[07:35] Maya Patel: Right.

[07:36] Stephanie Nguyen: Based on the run you did — 2.3k output tok/sec average — we can estimate what pool size you’re effectively using and how much headroom you have. I’ll send a write-up but I think we should price out 3 options: a smaller pool if you split routes and accept queueing for background, a mid pool that meets the interactive SLO during burst, and a larger pool for event peaks.

[07:57] Maya Patel: That’s what we need.

[08:00] Connor Lee: Can we compare to what we’d do on SageMaker? That’s what leadership is used to.

[08:05] Stephanie Nguyen: Yup. We can map it to “equivalent always-on GPU capacity” versus autoscaling. Dedicated is reserved, so it’s predictable.

[08:14] Elena Ruiz: We also use OpenAI for some fallback right now.

[08:18] Stephanie Nguyen: Got it. We can discuss a hybrid, but if Dedicated meets your p99 you might not need the fallback.

[08:26] Markus Klein: Also on fallback, our platform can do model fallback but for the PoC let’s keep it simple.

[08:33] Connor Lee: Agreed.

[08:35] Markus Klein: Going back to tuning: I’d like you to re-run the benchmark with a few changes. We should keep prompt set constant, fixed seed if possible. Then test:
- max_batch_tokens higher, maybe 16384,
- max_num_seqs 24 instead of 32,
- and queue delay target 10ms.

[09:00] Connor Lee: Okay. We can do that.

[09:02] Elena Ruiz: How do we set queue delay? Is that exposed?

[09:06] Ethan Park: We can set it in the deployment config. For PoC I can apply it on our side and let you know the exact values.

[09:14] Elena Ruiz: Great.

[09:16] Maya Patel: Does increasing max batch tokens increase memory use?

[09:19] Markus Klein: It can. But because you’re already near 82%, we’ll be careful. Caching might actually reduce compute but not always memory, depends.

[09:28] Connor Lee: We also saw a weird issue where two requests just like… stalled and then resumed.

[09:34] Markus Klein: That could be GC on your side or client backpressure, but it also can be queue starvation if one long decode hogs.

[09:43] Ethan Park: Do you have logs with request IDs?

[09:46] Elena Ruiz: Yes, we can share.

[09:48] Stephanie Nguyen: Let’s do that offline, we’ll pull server-side traces.

[10:00] Maya Patel: One more question: if prefix caching is on, is it safe with multi-tenant? Like, are we sharing with other customers?

[10:07] Ethan Park: On Dedicated, it’s only your pool. So no cross-customer cache.

[10:12] Maya Patel: Perfect.

[10:14] Stephanie Nguyen: And for prod, do you require VPC peering or is IP allowlist okay?

[10:19] Maya Patel: For initial, IP allowlist is okay. Long-term we want VPC.

[10:24] Elena Ruiz: Yeah, security will ask, but it’s not a blocker for the pilot.

[10:28] Stephanie Nguyen: Helpful. That means we can move faster.

[10:32] Markus Klein: Connor, on your test harness, are you using streaming parsing correctly? Sometimes TTFT includes client processing time.

[10:39] Connor Lee: I think so, but maybe. We measure when first chunk arrives.

[10:43] Markus Klein: Okay, that’s fine. Once we enable server-side breakdown, we’ll cross-check.

[10:50] Ethan Park: Also the region — you’re hitting us-west, correct?

[10:53] Elena Ruiz: Yes.

[10:55] Ethan Park: Your users are mostly us-east?

[10:57] Maya Patel: Mixed, but yes, more east.

[11:00] Ethan Park: That alone can add like ~70-90ms. Not p99 7 seconds, but it matters.

[11:07] Maya Patel: For prod we might want us-east.

[11:10] Stephanie Nguyen: Noted. That could be part of the commit: capacity in us-east.

[11:17] Markus Klein: Okay, if it’s okay, I’ll suggest we define success criteria for week 2:
1) p95 TTFT under 2 seconds at 200 concurrency,
2) p99 under 4 seconds,
3) error rate under 0.5%.

[11:33] Maya Patel: That’s good.

[11:35] Connor Lee: If caching works, maybe p95 will be way better.

[11:39] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[11:41] Stephanie Nguyen: On commit sizing, Maya, do you have a sense of Q2 event peak? Like worst day.

[11:48] Maya Patel: For the end-of-quarter event, we expect 3x daily volume for like 48 hours.

[11:54] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay, and concurrency? Any guess.

[11:57] Elena Ruiz: Concurrency could spike to 400-500 for short periods.

[12:02] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. I’ll incorporate that as “event headroom”. We might propose a base commit plus a burst option.

[12:10] Maya Patel: Is burst like on-demand GPUs?

[12:13] Stephanie Nguyen: Sometimes, yes, depending on region capacity. We can talk through what’s realistic. But baseline commit is reserved.

[12:21] Connor Lee: Leadership will ask: can we do smaller commit now and expand later.

[12:26] Stephanie Nguyen: Yes. Contracts can be structured to ramp. Also, we can start with a 3-month pilot commit if procurement allows, then annualize.

[12:35] Maya Patel: Good.

[12:37] Markus Klein: Coming back to batching: one more nuance. If your burst is 300 requests in 20 seconds, that’s 15 RPS. With long prompts, prefill dominates. With caching you reduce prefill, so you can handle that RPS with fewer GPUs.

[12:55] Connor Lee: Makes sense.

[12:57] Elena Ruiz: Does caching help with privacy? Like are prompts stored?

[13:01] Ethan Park: The cache is ephemeral in memory. Not written to disk by default. For Dedicated, it stays in your environment. We can share exact retention semantics.

[13:10] Elena Ruiz: Please do. Our security team will ask.

[13:13] Stephanie Nguyen: We’ll send that.

[13:15] Maya Patel: Also, any risk it serves the wrong cache entry?

[13:19] Ethan Park: It’s keyed on the exact tokenized prefix. If there’s a mismatch, it’s a miss. It doesn’t approximate.

[13:27] Maya Patel: Great.

[13:30] Markus Klein: Okay, let’s do a quick recap on the benchmark you’ll run. Connor, you’ll re-run with the updated deployment settings we push, same prompt set, capture p50/p95/p99 TTFT, total tok/sec, and error codes.

[13:46] Connor Lee: Yes.

[13:47] Markus Klein: And if possible include server timestamps so we can align.

[13:52] Connor Lee: Okay.

[13:53] Stephanie Nguyen: And we’ll send pricing/commit options. Maya, what format is easiest? A one-pager with assumptions?

[14:00] Maya Patel: Yes. And include like “if you split routes” scenario.

[14:04] Stephanie Nguyen: Will do.

[14:06] Elena Ruiz: Also can we talk about monitoring? We want to put alerts on p99.

[14:12] Ethan Park: In the console we have latency dashboards per route. For dedicated, you can also export metrics to your Prometheus, but that’s a bit more setup.

[14:21] Elena Ruiz: For PoC we can use console.

[14:24] Ethan Park: Great.

[14:26] Markus Klein: Another thought: set a max generation for interactive route lower than 512, like 256. That will reduce tail decode.

[14:34] Maya Patel: We can do that. Some requests need long, but that’s rare.

[14:38] Connor Lee: We can separate. Yeah.

[14:40] Stephanie Nguyen: Perfect.

[14:42] (crosstalk)

[14:43] Elena Ruiz: Sorry, one more, when we saw p99 7 seconds, was the system shedding? Like any 429?

[14:50] Connor Lee: No 429s. Mostly just slower.

[14:53] Markus Klein: That suggests it’s queueing rather than explicit rate limit.

[14:58] Ethan Park: Or a few long sequences blocking. But we’ll verify with traces.

[15:04] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay. We’re at time. Let’s lock next steps.

[15:08] Stephanie Nguyen: Markus will send the recommended settings by tomorrow, Ethan will enable prefix caching on the PoC deployment, Connor will re-run the load test and share results by Monday, and I’ll send the commit sizing options by Monday as well.

[15:23] Maya Patel: Sounds good.

[15:25] Connor Lee: Yep.

[15:26] Elena Ruiz: Thanks.

[15:28] Ethan Park: Thanks all.

[15:30] Markus Klein: Thank you.

[15:32] Stephanie Nguyen: Great, talk next week.

---
Note: Transcript may contain inaccuracies due to automated speech recognition. Names/technical terms (KV cache, max_num_seqs, batch tokens) may be inconsistently transcribed.
